March. António, Ion Mărgărit’s son, has landed in Bucharest. Ana and Mihai are driving him to Grandpa Gheorghe’s village. On the way, António tells them about his father’s life.
António, did your father ever tell you why he left Romania?
Just once, when I was twenty. It was a winter night and he’d had a little port wine. He told me that after the war, while the others were going back to their villages, people were looking for him.

Because of the photos. At the front he had taken hundreds of pictures. Some showed things the new government didn’t want anyone to see. One day a friend warned him they were going to come and arrest him.
As soon as night fell, he left the house without anyone seeing him. He didn’t even say goodbye to Vasile and Gheorghe. He thought that if he told them, he would put them in danger.

Yes. He crossed the border on foot, at night. After a few months he reached Italy, and from there, by boat, Portugal. He had nothing with him: just his camera and the negatives, hidden in the lining of his coat.
And he never tried to come back?
For years he couldn’t. And when he finally could have, he was already too old. He always said he’d come back the following year. He died in 1999, without ever having come back.
Well, today he’s coming back a little, with you.
(smiles and touches his jacket pocket) Yes. I have it here. The photo of the three of them.

Imagine a film: the imperfect is the set, the indefinido is the action, the pluperfect is a flashback.
When the main verb is in the past, the conjunctions that take the subjunctive (ch. 40, 41) take the IMPERFECT subjunctive:
He left without anyone seeing him.
He hid the negatives so they wouldn’t find them.
He left before the police came.
He hugged him as if he were his brother.
He told him to wait until he came back.

“Cuando / en cuanto / hasta que” with a REAL past action → indicative: «En cuanto se hizo de noche, salió». The subjunctive only appears if the action was still in the future at that moment: «Esperó hasta que se hiciera de noche» (variant) / «hasta que se hizo de noche» (fact).

An extract from an old article, from 1985, in a Portuguese newspaper, translated into Spanish by António.
When Ion Mărgărit arrived in Porto in 1948, he didn’t speak a word of Portuguese. He had slept in stations, on boats and in churches.
After a year, he found work at a small photo studio on Rua das Flores. He swept the floor and developed other people’s photos.
Ten years later, he came to own the studio. For four decades he photographed weddings, christenings and families from all over the city.
His customers say he had a gift: he made people smile as if they were in front of an old friend. He always gave the same answer: “Well, in every face I’m looking for two friends I lost”.
¿Dónde había dormido Ion antes de llegar a Oporto?
El dueño del estudio de fotografía
¿A quién buscaba Ion en cada cara?

Grandpa Gheorghe’s village was three hours from Bucharest, at the end of a narrow road that climbed through the hills. By the time they arrived, it was already getting dark. It was cold, the sky was violet, and white smoke that smelled of firewood rose from the chimneys.

António hadn’t said anything for the last hour of the drive. He looked out of the window at the fields, the wells, the horse-drawn carts, as if he were trying to recognise something he had never seen. His father had described those landscapes to him hundreds of times. Now, at last, they were in front of his eyes.

Grandpa’s house was small, with a tin roof and a vine that covered the whole yard. At the gate, leaning on his stick, a very thin old man was waiting for them, in a black coat that was too big and a felt hat. He had been waiting there, as the neighbour told them later, since four in the afternoon.

António got out of the car slowly. He was seventy-six and his knees ached after the journey. For a few seconds the two men looked at each other without moving, ten metres apart, as if neither dared take the first step.
Grandpa Gheorghe spoke first. He said something in Romanian, very quietly. Mihai, who was beside him, translated without being able to stop his voice trembling.
“He says you have your father’s eyes. That as soon as he saw you getting out of the car, he knew you were Ion’s son.”

António took two steps. Then three more. And when he reached the old man, he did something nobody expected: he took off his hat, bent down and kissed his hand, as children in Portuguese villages did with their grandparents.

Grandpa Gheorghe dropped his stick and hugged him. They stayed like that for a long time, two old men embracing at the gate of a country house, while the neighbour wiped her tears with her apron and a dog barked in the distance.

Inside, in the kitchen, by the wood stove, António finally took the photo out of his jacket pocket. He had wrapped it in a silk handkerchief. He put it on the table, next to the other one, the one Grandpa Gheorghe had given Mihai and Ana two years earlier.

They were almost identical. The same rock. The same afternoon light. The same uniforms that were too big. In Gheorghe’s there were two soldiers. In António’s, three: on the left, a thin boy with a huge smile, holding a small camera.

“He took it with the self-timer,” António explained. “My father said it was the only photo he was in. He put the camera on a crate, pressed the button and ran to sit next to his friends before it went off.”
Grandpa Gheorghe laughed, for the first time all afternoon. A young lad’s laugh on a ninety-four-year-old face.
“I remember,” he said. “He fell over as he ran. That’s why he’s got that crazy face. Vasile and I laughed so hard that the lieutenant made us clean the latrines for a week.”

They talked until very late. Mihai translated from Romanian into Spanish, and Ana from Spanish for António, who understood almost everything, because, as he put it, Spanish and Portuguese were “cousins who argue but love each other”. Sometimes nobody needed to translate anything: a look or a hand on a hand was enough.

Grandpa Gheorghe told them what had happened in the village the morning after Ion disappeared. Two men in leather coats had come from the city and searched his house. They had questioned all the neighbours. They had interrogated him and Vasile for two days. They didn’t know anything, so they couldn’t say anything. And that, he understood now, was why Ion hadn’t said goodbye to them.

“For fifty years I thought he left without saying goodbye because he didn’t care about us,” said Grandpa, looking at the photo. “And it turns out he left like that because he cared about us too much.”

António then told him what his father had said on that single winter night: that he had left the village before dawn, that he had passed Gheorghe’s house and seen a light in the window, and that he had nearly knocked on the door. That he didn’t, so that when they came to ask, his friends could tell the truth.
“I was awake that night,” Grandpa said very quietly. “My mother was ill. If he had knocked, I would have opened the door.”
Nobody said anything for a long time. All you could hear was the fire in the stove.

The next morning, Grandpa Gheorghe asked to be taken somewhere. He wouldn’t say where. They all got into the car and, following his directions, took a dirt track that led out of the village towards the forest. After ten minutes, Grandpa raised his hand: there.

At the side of the track, among grass still yellow from winter, was a big grey rock, rounded on top, like a natural bench. Ana recognised it straight away, although she had never seen it in real life. It was the rock from the two photos.
The regiment had camped there for a week, one summer during the war, before marching off to the front. Since then, the rock hadn’t moved a single centimetre. It was the people who had changed.

It was Ana who had the idea. She asked Mihai for his phone, put it on the car bonnet, found the self-timer and asked the two old men to sit on the rock. Grandpa Gheorghe on the right, where he had always been. António on the left, in his father’s place. And in the middle, Vasile’s empty place.
“You sit in the middle,” Grandpa told Mihai. “You’re his grandson. You have his hands.”

Mihai did as he was told. Ana pressed the button and ran out of the frame. Ten, nine, eight… And just before it went off, Grandpa Gheorghe, without warning, raised his hat in the air, exactly as he had done a lifetime ago in the other photo.
The photo came out a little blurred. But all three of them were smiling like young lads.
António stayed in the village for five days. Before going back to Portugal, he gave Mihai a small wooden box. Inside was his father’s camera, an old Leica, with a leather case worn by the years.
“My father always said the camera had to go back to Romania,” he explained. “He never got to. But the camera has.”

Mihai knew exactly who to give it to. That very week, Ion Mărgărit’s camera changed hands for the last time: it went to Andrei, the Fine Arts student, who held it for a whole minute without saying anything, as if he had been given something alive.
His first photo with it was of the little walnut tree in the garden, which that March morning had put out three green leaves for the first time.

That night, back in Bucharest, Ana printed the new photo from the rock and took it to the wooden box under the floor. She put it with the others: Grandma Ileana’s letter, the silver ring, the photo of the two soldiers and now the one of three. Mihai watched her from the living-room doorway, with Rosa Elena asleep in his arms.
“Do you realise?” Ana said softly. “This box has been under our feet all this time, and every year it has another story. As if the house didn’t want us to leave without having heard them all.”

Mihai didn’t answer. But Ana saw how he looked at the living room, the walls, the iron balcony, like someone looking at something they’re afraid of losing. There were three months left until his contract ended. And neither of them yet dared to say out loud what they were thinking.

After returning to Portugal, António writes to Mihai.
Dear Mihai: I got home on Tuesday. As soon as I opened the door, I put the photo from the rock next to my father’s portrait.
All my life I thought my father had lost his friends for ever. Now I know they hadn’t forgotten him either.
My grandchildren have asked me to teach them Romanian. I told them that first they have to learn to say “Vin” like me.
Give Grandpa Gheorghe a hug from me. Tell him that, God willing, I’ll come back in the summer, before the grapes on his vine dry up.

My grandmother was born in 1940 in a village in Moldova. She was the eldest of seven children and, as her mother worked in the fields, she looked after the little ones.
At eighteen she met my grandfather at a village dance. He promised he would come back for her after his military service.
Two years later, he came back. She had already turned down three suitors, without her parents understanding why.
As soon as she saw him come into the yard, she ran out as if she were fifteen.
